blocks.text: When we place an element of area in an electric field, some of the lines of force pass through it (Fig. 9.10). The number of the field lines passing through a certain element of area is known as electric flux through that area. It is usually denoted by Greek letter φₑ. For example, the electric flux φₑ through the area A in Fig 9.10 is 4 while the flux through B is 2.

blocks.alt: Magenta field lines run upward and spread apart. Near the bottom, where they are close together, a small yellow area A is crossed by 4 lines. Higher up, where they are farther apart, an equal yellow area B is crossed by 2 lines.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.10: Electric flux through a surface normal to E (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.10).

blocks.text: In order to give a quantitative meaning to flux, the field lines are drawn such that the number of field lines passing through a unit area held perpendicular to field lines at a point represent the intensity E of the field at that point.

blocks.alt: Three panels with magenta field arrows E pointing right. (a) Maximum: a green area stands upright across the field and its vector A points right, along E. (b) Minimum: the area lies flat, parallel to the field, and A points straight up. (c) The area is tilted so that A makes an angle theta with E; a yellow dashed strip beside it, labelled A cos theta, is its projection perpendicular to E.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.11: (a) Maximum; (b) Minimum; (c) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.11).

blocks.text: Usually, the element of area is represented by a vector area A whose magnitude is equal to the surface area A of the element and whose direction is along normal to the area.
